story.headline: Australia’s central bank raised rates to the highest since 2008, but three of nine members wanted to wait and Governor Michele Bullock gave no hint of more, so the Aussie slipped below 70 US cents.

reads.policy: Australia raised rates overnight, but a split vote and a cautious governor suggest it may be near the top. Britain is still expected to hike on Thursday, and most other big central banks still lean toward higher rates. Currencies are moving on hints about what comes after each hike, not the hikes themselves.
reads.growth: Factories started the autumn strongly in the US and Britain, and euro-area industry kept growing. Solid growth gives central banks room to keep raising rates, which supports the dollar and the pound. Australia is the soft spot, with a weakening job market behind its central bank’s caution.
reads.inflation: Cheaper oil has eased one of the main forces pushing prices up, but inflation is still well above target in most big economies. Australia’s central bank now expects inflation to stay high until late 2027. Euro-area figures on Wednesday are the week’s main inflation test.
reads.risk: Markets were calm but cautious before the US midterm elections. Limited US strikes on Iranian targets reminded investors that peace talks are not a deal, and a slide in AI-linked shares is still weighing on the mood. The dollar firmed slightly and the Swiss franc kept its gains as a shelter.
reads.tot: Oil steadied after one of its biggest one-day falls of the war. That leaves exporters like Canada with less support than a week ago and importers like Japan and the euro area with a smaller bill. A setback in talks could send prices back up fast.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and they are also betting against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Their large bets on gold are shrinking. New figures arrive Friday.
reads.fiscal: France’s debt worries, with two rating firms on negative outlook, keep a weight on the euro. France’s parliament votes on the revenue side of its budget today, and Canada presents its budget on Thursday.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and others have since called for more. Markets still see a December hike as likely, though cheaper oil eases some of the pressure.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and a strong factory survey shows the economy can take higher rates.
fed.watch: The US job openings figures Tuesday, the ISM services survey on Wednesday and Friday’s October jobs report: strong figures would firm up a December hike.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. But the economy has stalled, and cheaper oil weakens the case for a second hike soon.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, a bit less than even odds.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation and the bank raised its forecasts sharply, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem’s speeches Tuesday and Thursday, Canada’s budget on Thursday and October jobs figures on Friday, plus oil prices.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, but it says more tightening is likely, and markets lean toward a December hike. Saturday's election adds uncertainty for the kiwi.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, and firms say they plan to raise prices more.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand job figures at 3:45 PM CT Tuesday, the general election on Saturday, November 7, and the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. Cheaper oil helps the euro area but also eases the price pressure behind that hike.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, and factory costs are rising at their fastest since May.
ecb.watch: Euro-area inflation for October at 4:00 AM CT Wednesday, France’s budget vote Tuesday, and ECB President Christine Lagarde’s speech on Thursday.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, with one member voting to hike, and said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. Governor Kazuo Ueda named no date, but a December hike looks likely and would give the yen some support.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy and the jobs market tight.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech at 10:00 AM CT Friday, Japanese wage and price figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three of nine members wanted to wait. Governor Michele Bullock gave no hint of more, so the Aussie slipped.
rba.priced: December: no move expected; the hike may be the last for now.
rba.why: Inflation has run hotter than the bank expected and will stay above its target until late 2027, but a weakening job market argues for caution.
rba.watch: Australian jobs and inflation figures before the December 8 decision, and the Chinese yuan, which the Aussie often follows.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, its first hike since 2023, and the debate is already about December. Strong factory figures make the hike easier to justify.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, and factory prices are climbing faster.
boe.watch: The decision and Monetary Policy Report at 6:00 AM CT Thursday, November 5: any hint about December matters more than the hike itself.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation is low, so the franc mostly moves on global fear and calm.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is below target, so the bank has no reason to raise rates while others do.
snb.watch: Swiss inflation figures for October, out early Tuesday, Chairman Martin Schlegel’s speech on Thursday, and the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Cheaper oil eases some of that pressure.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, which keeps US rates high.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, though cheaper oil could start to ease it.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is uneven, energy imports cost more, and France's debt worries weigh on it. Cheaper oil and a likely European Central Bank hike in December give it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is uneven: France shrank over the summer, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Prices are rising fast in Italy and France, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out, though prices have fallen sharply this week.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: Two of the three big rating firms now have France on negative outlook, which keeps investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound scores well because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, inflation is high and factories are busy.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, with factories at their busiest in two years, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the pound, so a firm Bank of England could force them to buy it back.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. The Bank of Japan says inflation has reached its goal, so a December hike could start to change that.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is still far below others', though it says inflation has reached its goal, which points to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, and Tokyo's warnings limit how weak it gets.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country; cheaper oil would ease that.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators holding unusually big bets on the yen, which could unwind fast if it weakens.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is below target, which keeps the Swiss National Bank from raising rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, and it was the strongest major currency as oil fell and tech shares slid on Monday.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because Australia’s rates are now the highest among major economies and it sells resources abroad. But the central bank hinted it may pause after its latest hike, and a weakening job market is a drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest of the major banks, though it hinted it may now pause.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected and is set to stay high until late 2027.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money in, though oil’s sharp fall trims that.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the Aussie, so good news could force them to buy it back.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and oil brings money in. Growth is the soft spot, and oil's sharp fall trims its support, though trade-deal hopes helped it hold up.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and may do so again in December, which narrows the gap with US rates.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money in, though oil has fallen sharply on hopes of an end to the Iran war.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is weak after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, and Saturday's election adds uncertainty. A steady services sector and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, and business confidence rose in October.
notes.risk: The kiwi has held up reasonably well through recent share market swings.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so good news could force them to buy it back.
